The project is built around a native code Forth compiler that is deployed as a position independent shellcode. It provides a platform for remote code execution, useful in information security contexts.

The primary use case for EvilVM is to deploy the agent on a remote system, and interact with it. The language’s outer interpreter is presented as an interactive shell or REPL, and the system provides the capability to deliver code to the agent, which is compiled, and added to the hyperstatic global environment.

trendStories.title: 人工智能没有智慧，你也不会有
trendStories.originalTitle: AI Has No Wisdom and Neither Will You
trendStories.fullContent:
September 22, 2026 | 5 minutes | Comments

In the past month alone I’ve heard these phrases:

Certainly the industry is transforming, however, the people and organizations falling into the trap of no longer reading and writing code only do so at their peril.

Fact is, vibe-coded projects devolve over time into an unmaintainable mess. The reason is simple, yet hard to fix: code maintainability and good architecture don’t have good measurements that we can apply, because it takes months, years even, to notice the effects of bad architecture or of unmaintainable code.

We can certainly define bad code: code that’s hard to read, hard to understand, hard to evolve for whatever the future throws our way. The kind of code in which changing one thing breaks the program in very non-deterministic ways, or breaks the logic somewhere else, far removed from your change, resembling the “butterfly effect”. The kind of code where adding a feature means a serious undertaking due to changing code in multiple places and still forgetting to patch everything, thus getting inconsistencies. Code in which the invariants of the design aren’t clear, with its authors no longer being around to guard against violations and ensure some coherence. Code that is hard to test, requiring mocks and exposing implementation details, leading to fragile tests that end up preventing meaningful refactoring.

And yet, we know it as a fact that noticing bad code takes time. Months, years. Of course, the experienced software engineers have a nose that can detect code smells and can take action long before the bad effects can be observed.

The proficient developers, the experts, rely on their intuition built with sweat and tears, working long hours trying to debug and fix production issues, swearing to never again be so foolish as to repeat past mistakes. It’s the kind of intuition that can’t really be made into a list of rigid rules, because everything is context-dependent. Experts are incompatible with the same rules and recipes that make beginners more productive. Experts don’t follow the rules, they make the rules.

And so we have a problem…

For one, AI is not trained on what it means for code to be maintainable. For instance, any reinforcement learning done needs a reward signal that can be measured immediately, not in months or years. The AI learns rules from rulebooks meant for beginners. The AI notices patterns from code in the wild and let’s be honest, most code in the wild is pretty bad. There is no fitness function you can define for maintainable code, at least not one that we can discern, otherwise it would’ve been baked into our linters.

Have you noticed how terrible is the AI at “simplifying” code? Yes, the SOTA models. It can’t even define functions properly, choosing to split functions into smaller functions that are not actually reusable. Extracting a smaller function from a bigger function is a very bad choice if, to understand the bigger function, you have to also read the implementation of the extracted smaller function. Defining reusable and clarifying functions is an art form, an art that takes mastery. Most developers, being still “advanced beginners” in the Dreyfus model, are not able to define good, clarifying, reusable functions and neither does the AI currently.

This wouldn’t be so bad if people would still be in control and learn from those mistakes. But we are seeing a trend of people relying on AI to write, and even read code.

Those people will never reach mastery, because they no longer make choices, they no longer take responsibility for mistakes in coding and no longer learn from those mistakes. It’s the AI that’s making mistakes now, the AI doesn’t learn from those mistakes, and neither are the people relying on AI for coding.

Don’t get me wrong, I think LLMs are a great tool. I’m no Luddite, I’ve integrated AI in my everyday work, while actually teaching my colleagues what I’ve learned. I gladly use LLMs to take care of all the boring, soul-sucking shit we have to deal with. I’m also enjoying the efficiency benefits that I’m seeing. But at the end of the day, it’s just a tool, and like all other revolutions, its light will also fade; IMO, it already is, as right now tech news is frankly quite boring.

People are actually terrible at making predictions. I believe the future will surprise all of us. But, I’m going to make a prediction of my own…

In the future we will see more and more companies proudly boasting their “NO-AI” policy as a competitive advantage. And they will be right.

“But automated assembly lines are always more efficient” people say, except that the software industry is special, because we’ve always done automation at scale, everything we do is automation, LLMs are not the only means for it, and depending on context, it may actually be a distraction. “Coding isn’t solved” in any meaningful sense. Sure, you can instruct the LLM to build you a C/C++ compiler, or you can just clone GCC or LLVM, and you’d get a better C/C++ compiler, for free, too. And maybe there are better ways to spend our time and resources than reinvent the same CRUD apps (human needs and desires are infinite, there’s no shortage of new goals to work on).

If people and companies don’t start being responsible about its use, there will be consequences.
trendStories.fullTranslation:
2026年9月22日｜5分钟｜评论

仅在过去一个月里，我就听到了这些说法：

“毫无疑问，这个行业正在转型；然而，那些掉进不再阅读和编写代码这一陷阱的人和组织，终将自食其果。”

“事实是，凭感觉编写的项目会随着时间推移，逐渐沦为一团无法维护的乱麻。原因很简单，却很难解决：代码的可维护性和良好架构没有我们可以采用的有效衡量指标，因为糟糕架构或不可维护代码所造成的影响，往往要经过数月、甚至数年才能显现。”

我们当然可以定义什么是糟糕的代码：难以阅读、难以理解，也难以应对未来各种变化而演进的代码。这类代码中，改动一个地方可能以极其不可预测的方式破坏整个程序，或者破坏远离改动点的其他地方的逻辑，近似于“蝴蝶效应”。这类代码中，添加一个功能意味着一项艰巨的工作：需要在多个地方修改代码，却仍可能漏掉某些补丁，从而造成不一致。这样的代码，其设计中的不变量并不清晰；而它的作者可能已经不在了，无法防止违规情况、确保整体协调。这样的代码也很难测试，需要使用模拟对象并暴露实现细节，最终导致脆弱的测试，反过来阻碍有意义的重构。

然而，我们知道一个事实：发现糟糕的代码需要时间——数月，甚至数年。当然，经验丰富的软件工程师有一种能够察觉代码异味的直觉，在糟糕后果显现之前很久就能采取行动。

熟练的开发者、专家们，依靠的是用汗水和泪水铸就的直觉。他们长时间工作，努力调试并修复生产环境中的问题，发誓再也不会愚蠢到重蹈覆辙。这种直觉实际上无法被整理成一套僵化的规则，因为一切都取决于具体情境。专家与那些能让初学者提高生产力的同一套规则和配方并不相容。专家不遵循规则，他们制定规则。

于是，我们遇到了一个问题……

首先，人工智能并没有接受关于代码“可维护性”意味着什么的训练。比如，任何强化学习都需要一个能够立即衡量的奖励信号，而不是要等数月或数年才能衡量。人工智能从面向初学者的规则手册中学习规则。人工智能从现实世界中的代码里观察模式，而坦率地说，现实世界中的大多数代码都相当糟糕。你无法为可维护代码定义一个适应度函数，至少目前还无法定义一个我们能够辨识的适应度函数；否则，它早就已经被纳入代码检查工具中了。

你有没有注意到，人工智能在“简化”代码方面有多糟糕？没错，我说的是最先进的模型。它甚至无法恰当地定义函数，只会选择把函数拆分成更小的函数，而这些小函数实际上并不可复用。如果为了理解一个大函数，还必须阅读被提取出来的小函数的实现，那么从大函数中提取小函数就是一个非常糟糕的选择。定义出可复用且能澄清意图的函数是一门艺术，是需要精通的艺术。按照德雷福斯模型，大多数开发者仍处于“高级初学者”阶段，他们无法定义出优秀、清晰且可复用的函数；目前的人工智能也同样做不到。

如果人们仍然掌握控制权，并能从这些错误中学习，这本来不会是多么糟糕的事。但我们正在看到一种趋势：人们开始依赖人工智能来编写代码，甚至阅读代码。

这些人永远无法达到精通境界，因为他们不再做出选择，不再为编码中的错误承担责任，也不再从这些错误中学习。现在犯错的是人工智能；人工智能不会从这些错误中学习，而那些依赖人工智能编程的人也不会从中学习。

别误会我的意思，我认为大型语言模型是很棒的工具。我不是卢德分子；我已经把人工智能整合进日常工作，同时也在实际教同事们我所学到的东西。我很乐意让大型语言模型替我们处理那些不得不面对的、无聊而且耗尽灵魂的破事。我也很享受由此带来的效率提升。但归根结底，它只是一种工具；和所有其他革命一样，它的光芒也会逐渐消退。依我看，它已经开始消退了，因为如今的科技新闻坦率地说相当无聊。

人们实际上很不擅长做预测。我相信，未来会让我们所有人感到意外。不过，我要做出一个属于自己的预测……

未来，我们会看到越来越多的公司骄傲地把“禁止使用人工智能”政策当作竞争优势进行宣传。而且，它们会是对的。

人们会说：“自动化流水线总是更高效。”但软件行业很特殊，因为我们一直在大规模地进行自动化；我们所做的一切都是自动化，人工智能并不是实现自动化的唯一手段，而且根据具体情境，它实际上可能成为一种干扰。“编程已经被解决”——这句话在任何有意义的层面上都不成立。当然，你可以指示大型语言模型为你构建一个 C/C++ 编译器；但你也可以直接克隆 GCC 或 LLVM，这样你会得到一个更好的 C/C++ 编译器，而且还是免费的。也许，与其重新发明同样的 CRUD 应用，我们还有更好的方式来投入时间和资源（人类的需求和欲望是无限的，我们不缺新的目标去努力实现）。

如果人们和企业不开始对人工智能的使用负责，就会承担后果。

trendStories.title: 要闻：我刚刚发布了 Extralite 3.1.0 版本
trendStories.fullContent:
I’ve just released of Extralite version 3.1.0. This new release implements automatic caching of parametric queries, and updates the bundled SQLite to version 3.53.4.

Extralite is a fast and innovative SQLite wrapper for Ruby with a rich set of features. It provides multiple ways of retrieving data from SQLite databases, makes it possible to use SQLite databases in multi-threaded and multi-fibered Ruby apps, and includes a comprehensive set of tools for managing SQLite databases.

Extralite now automatically caches the underyling sqlite3_stmt object for any parametric query. Previously, when you ran the same SQL using Database#query_xxx with different parameters, each time the query ran Extralite would create a new sqlite3_stmt, which causes sqlite to repeatedly parse the same SQL over and over again. Now, when calling one of the Database#query_xxx methods (or Database#execute), Extralite will automatically cache the underlying sqlite3_stmt object and reuse it on repeated calls, thus reducing allocations and minimizing parsing overhead, letting you squeeze even more performance out of your SQLite-based app.

Previously, I’ve written about the advantages of working with relational databases by issuing raw SQL queries instead of using an ORM. Extralite is all about letting you do that easily and at the same time maximize performance. Here’s a simple example of code that does just that:

With automatic query caching, you don’t need to explicitly create prepared queries (using Database#prepare). You can just issue the same parametric SQL, and Extralite will do the work of caching the underlying query for you.

Extralite is designed to let you get the most out of your SQLite databases. It automatically sets your database up for using WAL and enforcing foreign key constraints (you can turn it off for legacy databases). It provides advanced features such as batch execution of parametric queries, savepoints, backups and changesets. And in addition, it is fast!

Extralite also lets you generate object graphs with indentity maps from query results using structured transforms, which lets you retrieve entities along with all their associations using a single query, without ever needing to use an ORM!

My goal for Extralite is to make it into a comprehensive tool for building apps on top of SQLite databases without using an ORM. I want it to be fast and simple to use. Following up on automatic query caching, I’d like to actually remove the Extralite::Query class that encapsulates a prepared query, since in my view automatic query caching already solves most of the value of prepared queries. Please let me know if you think this abstraction is necessary for your use case, I might change my mind.

trendStories.title: 要闻：Git 2.56 版本包含 700 多个非合并提交
trendStories.fullContent:
The Git 2.56 release contains something over 700 non-merge commits; it brings a number of nice improvements, but will not fundamentally change the Git experience for most users. One feature that offers some potential in that regard is the addition of the drop subcommand to the (still experimental) git history toolbox:

This command will cause the identified commit to be removed from the history of the current branch, replaying all commits that were added after it. It offers an easier way of removing an offending commit. Unfortunately, it still refuses to work if the history contains merge commits, making it unusable for many (or most) repositories.

The git status command will now suggest a git pull command to update a branch that is behind the branch it tracks. It still, though, will say that a branch is "up to date" even if it lags behind an (unfetched) remote tracking branch.

The git refs command exists to manipulate references at a low level; in 2.56, it has gained a number of new subcommands. Those commands, create, delete, update, and rename, perhaps surprisingly for Git, do exactly what their names suggest they would.

There are a number of minor usability tweaks. The new --delete-merged option to git branch will remove local branches that have been merged into their remote tracking branches. An attempt to delete a branch with git branch -d will fail, with a useful message, if that branch is being used for bisection. Attempts to lock the configuration file will be retried on failures, avoiding annoyance when multiple commands try to modify the file at once. git add has a new --resolved option that only adds files with merge conflicts that have been resolved.

Beyond that, there is the usual long list of bug fixes, refactorings, and performance improvements. All told, 2.56 looks like a solid release, but it also shows the signs of a project that is holding back much of its more significant work for the future. That leads to the question of what comes next.

In early September, Git maintainer Junio Hamano asked the community what the next release should be. Would it be best to put out the 3.0 release that the community has been working toward for some time, finishing the year on a high note? Or, instead, is there a need for one or more 2.x releases still before the 3.0 release can happen?

This is an important question, because 3.0 will contain a number of compatibility breaks that may make some users pause before upgrading. Of those, perhaps the most significant is the switch to using the SHA-256 hash function by default, rather than the SHA-1 hash that Git has used since the beginning. SHA-1 has long been deemed to be weak, which is worrisome for applications like Git. Hashes are used to identify every object (files, directory trees, commits) in the Git repository, and are used to verify the chain of commits leading to any given point. If SHA-1 can be broken, it can conceivably be used to modify the history of a repository in ways that are difficult or impossible to detect.

Git has long included defenses against the known SHA-1 attacks, and few people appear to be seriously worried about the potential for compromised repositories now. Still, it makes a lot of sense to move to a more secure hash function.

Non-experimental support for SHA-256 has existed in Git since the 2.42 release in 2023, though some of the glue for interoperating with older repositories has taken longer. The biggest concern that has kept the Git developers from moving to SHA-256 by default for some time now has been support (or the lack thereof) at the major forge sites. GitLab has had support since 2024, and Forgejo has support as well. The elephant that is still missing from this room, though, is GitHub; releasing a version of Git that creates GitHub-incompatible repositories is a worrisome prospect. It still is not clear when GitHub might add that support, but it is notable that brian m. carlson, a GitHub employee and a key developer behind the SHA-256 transition, responded to Hamano's question by saying that news on that topic was coming, and that that having the next release be 3.0 might be the best choice.

That said, carlson has posted one other change that he would like to see added before 3.0 comes out. While Git has always managed hexadecimal numbers (specifically, object IDs) as lower-case strings, it has also accepted upper-case IDs. That leads to situations where two seemingly different IDs (f00f00 and F00F00, say) are actually the same. Seemingly, bugs and security vulnerabilities have arisen from this ambiguity. So carlson wants to change Git's behavior to only accept IDs in lower case. That is a change that, seemingly, should not cause problems for too many users, but there is almost certainly somebody somewhere who relies on that behavior.

Another significant change that has been waiting for the 3.0 release is the switch to the "reftable" mechanism. A reference (more commonly "ref") in Git is an association between a name and an object in the repository; branches, tags, and remotes are all refs, for example. Git currently (by default) stores each ref as a file under .git/refs/ in the repository. If a repository contains a branch called foo, there will be a file, .git/refs/heads/foo, containing the ID of the commit at the head of that branch. There is also a mechanism to pull all of these refs together into a packed-refs file, which increases performance — to a point.

This mechanism works, but becomes increasingly inefficient as the number of refs grows. In some projects, the number of refs does indeed grow. According to the project's reftable documentation, the Android repository contains over 800,000 refs. At that scale, looking up refs, or determining whether any refs pointing to a specific commit exist, can be an expensive operation. Slowing down development can be a yellow-card-level annoyance, leading to a desire to do something about the refs.

The Git 2.45 release added reftables as a more efficient way of storing refs. It is a binary file optimized for both space efficiency and quick access. Since then, it has been possible to create a repository that uses a reftable rather than the old file-based mechanism, but that has never been the default. Switching to reftable should have no visible consequences (other than better performance) for users of Git itself, but it can be a problem for users of other software packages that access Git repositories. In his email, carlson mentioned libgit2 as a potential concern.

As it turns out, libgit2 will not be a blocker here; Patrick Steinhardt let it be known that he has added reftable support to libgit2, and that SHA-256 support had been enabled by default in August. So libgit2 should be ready for the Git 3.0 transition.

Finally, as mentioned by carlson, there is the Rust question. The project has added some trial support for code written in Rust, but has hesitated to make Rust mandatory for the building of Git. That, too, is expected to change in the 3.0 release; after that, any platform that does not have a working Rust compiler will be unable to upgrade.

After listing these concerns, carlson suggested that they probably should not hold up the 3.0 release:

Similarly, I am not aware of anyone who is seriously undertaking Rust support for platforms that do not already support it, so I don't think that should be a blocker, either.

That led to his conclusion that, most likely, designating the next release as 3.0 would be the best choice.

What will actually happen has not, yet, been announced publicly; that is waiting for Hamano to make a decision. As he put it: "this is not a popularity contest, nor is it even a democracy". In the nearly two weeks since his query was posted, though, there has been no strong opposition to moving into the 3.x era and leaving some of Git's early design decisions behind (though, naturally, repositories using SHA-1 and lacking reftables will continue to be fully supported). If the 3.0 release does not happen in 2026, it seems certain to show up shortly thereafter.

Ah, the fact that GitHub doesn't support SHA-256 almost makes me want to go and convert all my repos so they are harder to mirror to GitHub. 😛

Sorry/glad to be the bearer of bad/good news!

Very interesting to read (and I suspect the actual talk would have been more so) - it's not often you get to see that sort detail about Rust/C interoperability in such a well-established project.

Could you give a link? Thanks!

I think you can just open presentation.adoc

Just thinking out loud sorry.

This is the first thing that blew up for me when trying the repo linked from this comment. This was due to an unusual workflow (every repo I clone gets added to a parent module that indexes everything), but it is the kind of thing that would block popular repos from making the transition to sha256.

"A repo must use sha256 to reference sha256 submodules, but a sha256 repo can also reference sha1 submodules" would at least speed the transition along.

With the current submodule intolerance, the transition could work with every repo having both hashes. The major forges could handle it (configuring extensions.compatObjectFormat and generating v3 pack indexes with both hashes) but it would penalize everybody using git in a more federated way and needing to reference repos outside their control.

I've long wanted a way to distinguish integration branches from development branches. We currently enforce this by making everyone use fork-based workflows so as to not pollute the main repository (finally acknowledged by forges with their "only copy the HEAD branch" checkbox…that also ignores tags or any active release-maintenance branches). Only recently the obvious solution is to have refs/heads/ for integration branches and refs/topics/ for development branches.

Effects this would have:

It might not have to be enforced, but if there was the space to have another top-level namespace of refs to do so, defaults would still work well.

Git distinguishes annotated tags from unannotated; I think this is a similar concept. Perhaps it'd just need some kind of associated metadata to distinguish them? branch.<branch>.integration or something?

Ok, but I've come to prefer having roots of at least the data model in the base instead of forcing interaction through the forge to enforce things like this.

No-rewind enforcement based on "is integration" instead of doing server-side name-based enforcement

Given that you propose "is integration" to ultimately resolve to a ref name prefix check (i.e. "is refs/heads/"), it seems to me that you are suggesting to replace server-side name-based enforcement with... server-side name-based enforcement? :-)

Yes, the server would, ultimately, still be the enforcer. But your tools can say "hey, that rebase you did looks fishy; did you mean to create a topic instead of rebasing all of release-1.x onto main?" before you push.

trendStories.fullTranslation:
Git 2.56 版本包含 700 多个非合并提交；它带来了许多不错的改进，但对于大多数用户而言，并不会从根本上改变 Git 的使用体验。在这方面颇具潜力的一项特性，是在（仍处于实验阶段的）git history 工具箱中新增了 drop 子命令：

该命令将使指定的提交从当前分支的历史记录中被移除，并重新重放其后添加的所有提交。它为移除有问题的提交提供了一种更简便的方式。不幸的是，如果历史记录中包含合并提交，它仍然无法工作，这使得它在许多（或绝大多数）代码仓库中无法使用。

git status 命令现在会建议使用 git pull 命令来更新落后于其跟踪分支的本地分支。不过，即使分支落后于（尚未拉取的）远程跟踪分支，它仍然会显示分支处于“最新状态”（up to date）。

git refs 命令用于在底层操作引用；在 2.56 中，它增加了一系列新的子命令。这些命令包括 create、delete、update 和 rename，或许出乎 Git 的一贯常态，它们的功能正如其名称所示，名副其实。

新版本还带来了许多细节上的可用性调整。git branch 新增的 --delete-merged 选项将移除已合并到其远程跟踪分支的本地分支。如果某个分支正在被用于二分查找（bisect），尝试使用 git branch -d 删除该分支将会失败，并显示一条有用的提示信息。在锁定配置文件失败时将会进行重试，避免在多个命令同时尝试修改该文件时造成困扰。git add 新增了一个 --resolved 选项，该选项只添加已解决合并冲突的文件。

除此之外，还有常规的大量错误修复、重构和性能改进。总的来说，2.56 看起来是一个坚实稳定的版本，但它也显露出该项目正将许多更重大的工作留待将来的迹象。这就引出了一个问题：接下来会是什么？

9 月初，Git 维护者滨野纯（Junio Hamano）询问社区下一个版本应该是什么。是发布社区为之努力了一段时间的 3.0 版本、以此为这一年画上圆满句号最好？还是说，在 3.0 版本发布之前，仍需要发布一个或多个 2.x 版本？

这是一个重要的问题，因为 3.0 将包含许多破坏向后兼容性的改动，可能会让一些用户在升级前犹豫不决。在这些改动中，最重要的或许是默认改用 SHA-256 哈希函数，而不是 Git 从一开始就使用的 SHA-1 哈希。长期以来，SHA-1 一直被认为是不够安全的，这对于像 Git 这样的应用程序来说令人担忧。哈希值用于标识 Git 仓库中的每一个对象（文件、目录树、提交），并用于验证导向任意特定节点的提交链。如果 SHA-1 可以被破解，那么可以想象它可能被用来篡改仓库的历史记录，而且这种篡改将难以甚至无法被察觉。

Git 长期以来一直包含针对已知 SHA-1 攻击的防御机制，目前似乎很少有人严重担心仓库被篡改的潜在风险。尽管如此，转向更安全的哈希函数仍然十分有意义。

自 2023 年的 2.42 版本以来，Git 就已经具备了对 SHA-256 的非实验性支持，不过与旧仓库互操作的一些胶水层支持花费了更长时间。一段时间以来，阻碍 Git 开发者将 SHA-256 设为默认的最大顾虑，是主要代码托管平台（forge sites）的支持情况（或者说缺乏支持）。GitLab 自 2024 年起就提供了支持，Forgejo 也提供了支持。然而，房间里那头依然缺席的大象是 GitHub；发布一个会创建与 GitHub 不兼容的仓库的 Git 版本，是一个令人担忧的前景。目前尚不清楚 GitHub 何时可能会添加该支持，但值得注意的是，GitHub 员工、同时也是 SHA-256 转型背后的关键开发者 brian m. carlson 在回复滨野纯的问题时表示，关于该主题的消息即将到来，并将下一个版本定为 3.0 可能是最佳选择。

话虽如此，carlson 还提出了他希望在 3.0 发布之前添加的另一项变更。尽管 Git 一直将十六进制数（具体指对象 ID）作为小写字符串管理，但它也接受大写 ID。这导致了两个看似不同的 ID（例如 f00f00 和 F00F00）实际上是相同的情况。显然，这种模糊性引发了一些漏洞和安全弱点。因此，carlson 希望更改 Git 的行为，使其仅接受小写 ID。这一变更表面上看应该不会对太多用户造成困扰，但几乎可以肯定，某些地方一定有人依赖于这一行为。

另一个一直在等待 3.0 发布的重大变更是切换到“reftable”机制。Git 中的引用（通常称为“ref”）是名称与仓库中对象之间的关联；例如，分支、标签和远程跟踪分支都是引用。目前，Git（默认情况下）将每个引用作为文件存储在仓库的 .git/refs/ 目录下。如果仓库包含一个名为 foo 的分支，就会存在一个文件 .git/refs/heads/foo，其中包含该分支顶端提交的 ID。此外还有一种将所有这些引用汇总到 packed-refs 文件中的机制，这在一定程度上提升了性能。

这种机制能够正常工作，但随着引用数量的增加，其效率变得越来越低。在某些项目中，引用数量确实大幅攀升。根据该项目的 reftable 文档，Android 仓库包含超过 800,000 个引用。在如此庞大的规模下，查找引用或确定是否存在指向特定提交的引用，可能是一项极其昂贵的操作。开发速度变慢是一种黄牌警告级别的困扰，从而催生了对引用机制进行改造的愿望。

Git 2.45 版本引入了 reftable，作为一种更高效的引用存储方式。它是一种针对空间效率和快速访问都进行了优化的二进制文件。从那时起，创建使用 reftable 而非旧的文件机制的仓库已经成为可能，但这从未成为默认设置。对于 Git 本身的用户来说，切换到 reftable 应该不会产生可见的影响（除了更好的性能），但对于访问 Git 仓库的其他软件包的用户来说，这可能会成为一个问题。carlson 在其邮件中提到了 libgit2 这一潜在的顾虑点。

事实证明，libgit2 在这里不会成为阻碍；Patrick Steinhardt 透露，他已经为 libgit2 添加了 reftable 支持，并且 SHA-256 支持已在 8 月份默认启用。因此，libgit2 应该已经为 Git 3.0 的过渡做好了准备。

最后，正如卡尔森（carlson）所提到的，还存在 Rust 的问题。该项目已为用 Rust 编写的代码增加了一些试验性支持，但在将 Rust 列为构建 Git 的强制依赖方面一直犹豫不决。这一情况预计也将在 3.0 版本中发生改变；在此之后，任何没有可用 Rust 编译器的平台都将无法进行升级。
在列举了这些顾虑后，卡尔森表示，它们大概不应该阻碍 3.0 版本的发布：
“同样，我不知道有谁正在认真为那些尚不支持 Rust 的平台开展 Rust 支持工作，因此我认为这也不应成为阻碍因素。”
这使他得出结论：最有可能的是，将下一个版本命名为 3.0 会是最佳选择。
实际情况究竟如何尚未公开宣布；这正等待滨野（Hamano）做出决定。正如他所言：“这不是一场人气竞赛，甚至也不是一场民主投票”。不过，自他的疑问发布以来的近两周里，对于迈入 3.x 时代并摒弃 Git 早期的一些设计决策（当然，使用 SHA-1 且缺少 reftable 的仓库仍将得到完全支持），并没有出现强烈的反对意见。如果 3.0 版本没有在 2026 年发布，它似乎也必然会在其后不久面世。
啊，GitHub 不支持 SHA-256 这个事实，简直让我忍不住想去把自己所有的仓库都转换掉，这样它们镜像到 GitHub 就更困难了。😛

读起来非常有趣（我猜现场演讲可能会更加引人入胜）——在这样一个如此成熟的项目中，看到有关 Rust/C 互操作性的这种细节可不多见。

在尝试这条评论中链接的仓库时，这是第一个让我崩溃的地方。这是因为一种不寻常的工作流（我克隆的每个仓库都会添加到一个为所有内容建立索引的父模块中），但正是这类问题会阻碍热门仓库向 sha256 过渡。

长期以来，我一直想要一种能够区分集成分支（integration branch）和开发分支（development branch）的方法。我们目前通过强制每个人使用基于 fork 的工作流来做到这一点，以免污染主仓库（各托管平台最终通过其“仅复制 HEAD 分支”复选框承认了这一点……但这也忽略了标签或任何活跃的发布维护分支）。直到最近，显而易见的解决方案是在 refs/heads/ 下存放集成分支，在 refs/topics/ 下存放开发分支。

trendStories.title: 正确设计你的编程语言（2024）
trendStories.fullContent:
I just think we should have some ground rules for new programming languages and their configuration. Yʼknow?

Just some rambly thoughts on features I think you should include, or at least think about and not block yourself out of including. And other topics I am thinking about with no real answers yet.

Itʼs so ugly when you go to embed a multiline string into your code, and you realize that you’re going to have to close your eyes and pretend the current indentation level does not exist, as the raw contents take over the left gutter.

This is a solved problem. Dhall did a pretty good job of it (although I am not too fond of the escaping rules there), and Nix/Lix have similar rules.

I implemented similar logic for JavaScript template literals in Ve.dedent, I am very happy with it. And Iʼve tried my best for PureScript (and Python?), but not having the distinction between source and escaped/interpolated texts makes it much harder, and more of a tool that works for some cases than a systematic approach that it could be if it was baked in.

Indented multiline strings are just a thing that you can put a few extra hours of effort into fixing early, before it becomes a problem for your users and then you canʼt change without backwards compatibility issues.

File paths should be relative to the file theyʼre in, or to a well defined project root. This mostly applies to configuration, less so running programs (for which a working directory is usually fine), but like … imports should be predictable.

Notably, configuration files for both Docker Compose and Rustʼs Cargo get this wrong.

Again, you have to get it right up-front, or figure out solid plans for versioning. (But of course, programming languages that donʼt have the thought put in to get it right up front, usually donʼt have good enough versioning policies to deal with this either.)

Pick an extension or two, and stick to it! Remember that if youʼre a new language, youʼre a guest entering existing ecosystems by their good grace and should work on their terms.

Syntax highlighting, in IDEs and online code viewers/git forges, is mainly based on the file extension. And if you donʼt have a recognizable file extension, your users are going to have to work harder.

As one example, Bazel uses Starlark in files named WORKSPACE and BUILD and .bzl or .bazel. Starlark just has Python syntax highlighting, which is nice that you can use that.

But itʼs hard to convince your IDE to highlight them if thereʼs different extensions and extensionless file names. (Itʼs even harder if these names are configurable, but I donʼt think WORKSPACE and BUILD are?) Itʼs harder to grep through the files if you have to include all the forms that it can occur. And so on.

Another solved problem: allow trailing commas! (And possibly leading commas, if you feel like that … or actual bullet points.)

A lot of languages have made mistakes around numeric literals (wanting to add more prefixes or suffixes, but the path forward is blocked by backwards compatibility), or string/regex escapes (use delimited escapes like "\u{XXXX}"!), or keywords.

Itʼs more my personal opinion, but I dislike bare keywords. I think keywords should come with a sigil to clearly denote them as a keyword and allow extending the language with more keywords without breaking old code that used them as identifiers. Do you really think youʼll get the perfect set of keywords right the first time? … can you point to a programming language that did?

iterating on code as youʼre developing it, versus having a nice clean, pristine released version … theyʼre quite different things, and I think these workflows should be respected!

e.g. when developing, we often put web servers on different ports and/or LAN hosts, and use HTTP or self-signed HTTPS (or even file:/// in the few cases we can get away with it!), whereas in production it might be behind a reverse proxy under some specific route, and so on.

Versioning means a lot of things.

One of the problems that I havenʼt really seen solved before, is how to deal with code across versions.

Like, letʼs say that I want to have a migration script between versions of my released software. Well, I guess the code for it has to live in the later version – itʼs not like the previous version knew what was coming up. But how do you test it? You kind of need to check out the previous version of your code from source control, and have them both in parallel. (This is also something where the “development” and “release” modes are pretty separate!)

And in general, if youʼre expecting people to write libraries in your programming language, give them a sensible way to talk about versions. One of the cooler tools in this area are the ones that check a libraryʼs API (especially if it is typed!) to determine whether it should be a patch/minor/major release.

However, I must stress: version numbers are always going to be subject to judgment calls. They are an imperfect tool of communication, not a mathematically precise abstraction.

Oh another hobby horse: Please always include dates with your release version numbers! It doesnʼt have to be in the version number, but it should be easily accessible, displayed beside it or in a tooltip or on a canonical webpage. Itʼs nearly impossible to compare versions across software (languages, runtimes, packages, dependencies) without having a sense of release dates of it all.

This is part of a larger discussion around build systems and the like, but.

Iʼve never found it possible to retrofit detailed file watching onto build systems that didnʼt have it. Without, like, writing a whole Python program to go and parse files, reconstruct their dependency tree, make sure I know how each file is getting used and if it is relevant at all, reload the whole watcher if the configuration changes, and so on.

Like find/grep: itʼs much nicer if you can ask your build tool to tell you all the files to search through, and then you can ask if you want to include dependencies or not. (Also this listing of files/globs gives you a first step towards filewatching too, although (again) you really need proper integration to be able to account for added files, and changing configuration, and so on!)

Itʼs even better if you want to add proper code search, being able to distinguish your search terms in identifiers versus strings, or in types versus terms, and so on. Yeah ^.^
trendStories.fullTranslation:
我只是觉得，我们应该为新的编程语言及其配置制定一些基本规则。你懂的吧？

这只是一些杂乱的想法，列举了我认为你应该加入的特性，或者至少应该深思熟虑、别把自己未来加入这些特性的可能性给堵死的地方。还有一些是我正在思考、但尚未得出确切答案的话题。

当你准备在代码中嵌入一段多行字符串时，却发现必须闭上眼睛假装当前的缩进层级根本不存在，眼睁睁看着原始文本内容挤满代码编辑器的左侧边缘，这实在太难看了。

这是一个早已解决的问题。Dhall 在这方面做得相当不错（尽管我不太喜欢那里的转义规则），Nix/Lix 也有类似的规则。

我在 Ve.dedent 中为 JavaScript 模板字面量实现了类似的逻辑，效果让我非常满意。我也在 PureScript（以及 Python？）中竭尽全力尝试过，但由于缺乏源码文本与转义/插值文本之间的区分，这变得困难得多；最终它充其量只是一个在某些场景下能用的工具，而无法成为一种如同语言内置特性那样系统化的方案。

带缩进的多行字符串纯粹是一件可以在早期多花几个小时精力解决的事，何必等到它变成用户的痛点、让你陷入若不破坏向后兼容就无法更改的窘境呢。

文件路径应该相对于其所在文件，或者相对于定义明确的项目根目录。这主要适用于配置文件，对正在运行的程序影响较小（对于后者，使用工作目录通常就足够了），但话说回来……导入行为应该是可预测的。

值得注意的是，Docker Compose 和 Rust 的 Cargo 的配置文件在这点上都做错了。

再说一次，你必须从一开始就把它做对，或者构想出坚实的版本管理方案。（不过当然了，那些从一开始就没花心思把它做对的编程语言，通常也没有足够好的版本策略来应对这个问题。）

选定一两个文件扩展名，然后坚持用下去！请记住，如果你是一门新语言，你只是一位承蒙现有生态系统厚爱才得以进入的客人，理应按照既有规则行事。

无论在 IDE 还是在线代码查看器/Git 代码托管平台上，语法高亮主要都是基于文件扩展名来实现的。如果你的语言没有一个可识别的文件扩展名，你的用户就得付出更多折腾的代价。

举个例子，Bazel 在名为 WORKSPACE、BUILD 以及扩展名为 .bzl 或 .bazel 的文件中使用 Starlark。Starlark 恰好能复用 Python 的语法高亮，这一点确实很不错。

但如果存在多种不同的扩展名以及没有扩展名的文件名，你就很难说服你的 IDE 对它们进行高亮。（如果这些名称还可以自定义配置，那就更难了，不过我觉得 WORKSPACE 和 BUILD 应该不可配置吧？）如果你在 grep 检索文件时必须囊括所有可能出现的形式，搜索也会变得更难。诸如此类。

另一个早已解决的问题：允许尾随逗号（trailing commas）！（如果你喜欢的话，也可以允许前置逗号……甚至是真正的项目符号列表点号。）

许多语言在数值字面量（想要添加更多前缀或后缀，但前进的道路却被向后兼容性阻断）、字符串/正则转义（请使用带定界符的转义，比如 "\u{XXXX}"！），或关键字方面都犯过错误。

这更多是我个人的看法，但我讨厌无修饰的裸关键字（bare keywords）。我认为关键字应该自带某种指示符号（sigil），以明确标明它是关键字，这样既能方便日后扩展更多关键字，又不会破坏那些将这些词用作标识符的旧代码。你真的以为自己第一次就能把一整套关键字设计得完美无瑕吗？……你能找出一门真正做到了这一点的编程语言吗？

在开发过程中对代码进行迭代，与拥有一个整洁、无可挑剔的正式发布版本……这是截然不同的两码事，我认为这些不同的工作流理应受到尊重！

例如，在开发时，我们经常把 Web 服务器部署在不同的端口和/或局域网主机上，使用 HTTP 或自签名 HTTPS（或者在少数允许偷懒的情况下甚至直接用 file:///！）；而在生产环境中，它可能位于特定路由下的反向代理之后，等等。

版本控制包含很多层面的含义。

其中一个我从未真正见过被妥善解决的问题，就是如何处理跨版本的代码。

比方说，我想为已发布软件的不同版本之间编写一个迁移脚本。那么，这段代码显然必须存放在较新的版本中——毕竟之前的版本不可能预知未来的变化。但你该如何测试它呢？你差不多得从源码版本控制系统中把之前的版本检出，让两个版本并行存在。（这也是“开发”模式与“发布”模式截然不同的地方之一！）

总的来说，如果你希望人们用你的编程语言编写库，请给他们提供一种合理的版本交流方式。这方面比较酷的工具之一，是那些能够检查库的 API（尤其是带类型系统的语言！）以判定它应该是一个补丁（patch）、次要（minor）还是主要（major）版本的工具。

然而，我必须强调：版本号永远都取决于主观决断。它们是一种不完美的沟通工具，而非数学上精确的抽象。

噢，还有另一个我常挂在嘴边的话题：发布版本号时请务必附带日期！它不一定非要写在版本号本身里，但应该容易获取，比如展示在版本号旁边、工具提示（tooltip）中，或者权威官方网页上。如果对所有软件的发布日期毫无概念，你几乎不可能在跨软件（包括语言、运行时、软件包、依赖项）之间进行版本比对。

这是围绕构建系统等更大话题的其中一部分，不过：

我发现，对于原本没有细粒度文件监听（file watching）功能的构建系统，事后想要补丁式地添加这一功能是绝不可能做到的。除非你专门写一个完整的 Python 程序去解析文件、重建其依赖树、确保弄清每个文件是如何被使用的以及它到底是否相关、在配置更改时重载整个监听器，诸如此类。

就像 find/grep 一样：如果你可以直接让构建工具告诉你需要检索的所有文件，然后由你决定是否包含依赖项，体验就会好得多。（此外，列出这些文件/通配模式（globs）也是迈向文件监听的第一步，尽管话说回来，你确实需要进行适当的系统级集成，才能兼顾新增文件、配置变更等各种情况！）

如果你还想加入真正到位的代码搜索功能，能够区分搜索词究竟出现在标识符还是字符串中，或者出现在类型还是表达式项（terms）中等等，那就更棒了。没错 ^.^
